item.content:encoded:
As always, the creativity in ideas on how to "stop" it are appreciated and interesting :)

But that said, to answer the question inherent in this….that wouldn't work for the same reason various other things wouldn't work.

Let's put it this way…..pretend you're a cat. One day you see a red spot of light on the floor. You attempt to cover it up with your paw, but suddenly inexplicably it appears on top of your paw! In alarm you pull your paw away, and there it is again in the same place it was before. It begins to move. You chase it across the floor. Despite all your best efforts to capture it, nothing you do seems to have any effect upon it. You try every way you can think of to get rid of it or capture it, but no matter what, there it remains.

The red dot doesn't exist of its own accord. It is not an object to be captured, moved, or destroyed by the cat. It exists in that spot because it is being actively generated in that spot by a laser pointer.

Think of 225-1 and 225-2 in that context and it'll help with understanding why trying to do things to the spheres is a pointless endeavor. You need to find the source that is creating them where they are, not attack the visible representation of it.

item.content:encoded:
That's not the best case scenario. The Best Case Scenario is that one of them simply bounces away. Or since this is the SCP universe, they form a tuna sandwich. Or maybe they just disappear together. Since the foundation believes that they are 'linked,' there's probably some similarity between the two, possibly a common origin… and we've got no idea what that origin was or how these things work. Maybe they are controlled. Maybe they aren't.

Now then, we are assuming that the 'hovering' one (not sure why it says "orbit" when its only 7 meters off the ground) is actually NOT stationary and immovable, it actually moves with the Earth. As the Earth changes position, so does -it-. If it is -truly- anchored to the Earth with some infinite-strength invisible force, and it is truly infinitely invulnerable, then one would speculate that if some major force hits it, then that force will be transferred to the Earth.

So what will happen if they collide? Well, we should be able to ascertain SCP-225-2's mass from the "Lunar Impact Incident," but suffice to say, the moon is still there and its orbit is still the same. Additionally, we don't suffer any gravitational affects from SCP-225-2's drive-bys, so it's not nearly enough mass to really affect the Earth (like a Neutron Star core or a black hole or something). Worst case scenario, this thing hits the Earth-anchored SCP-225-1 and alters its orbit around the sun by a few centimeters. This is, of course, assuming that SCP-225-1 is anchored directly to the Earth's core, and not to some chunk of land below it, in which case, the the land would deform similar to a meteorite strike.

I'm all for anamolous SCPs. I'm not for using bad/stupid science to explain why two known Newtonian objects colliding will clearly equal THE END OF THE WORLD.

item.content:encoded:
If they strike each other, best case scenario is that they turn one another completely into energy. Whenever there's an explosion or what not, you're not actually turning all of the explosive into energy. It's extremely difficult to do. But this? There's nothing to 'give', to stop the conversion process. If or when they come into contact, all that mass(and inertia) is going to be let out. You're looking at a biosphere-ending explosion. And that's the best result.

The worse options? They hit and turn one another into energy…that then collapses in on itself. Then you've got a massive gravity well known as a black hole. That's not just a biosphere-killer, that's a planet-destroyer. I'm not even talking about it consuming the earth. It probably won't. But it'll fuck up the orbit of the moon and probably send it careening into the earth. Assuming that doesn't happen, and it just shoots the moon off into fuck-knows-where space, the orbit of the earth is permanently screwed. And that isn't even getting into the problems posed by the black hole ripping off our atmosphere.

There's even worse options too, but these are much harder to prove. Assuming they have infinite energy, and they hit…well, reality just ceased, because infinite means infinite, and that's much larger than our universe by an unquantifiable amount. Can't hold it.

item.content:encoded:
earthquakes are a poor measure to use, as most of the energy itself is involved in the relatively minor movement of trillions of tons of the earth's crust as opposed to destruction on the surface. asteroid impact likewise, as most of the force is directed into the ground. a nuclear explosion primarily affects things upon the surface, with the energy directed into the atmosphere and into destructive radiation. a 100 gigaton explosion may sound insignificant compared to the energy of other events(and yes i did these calculations too :P i love this stuff. i worked it out to be an explosion between 60 gigatons and 300 gigatons depending upon what the spheres were made of), but one has to look at the actual effects.

a 100 gigaton explosion would create an area of complete destruction with an approximately 75 mile radius. this would be a fireball 150 miles wide, meaning it would stretch beyond the atmosphere(along with causing seismic effects, though they would be comparatively minor), sending an airblast around the world and blowing a temporary hole in the atmosphere along with sending a significant portion of the atmosphere into space. the overall circle of destruction from the explosion itself would be approximately 1200 miles in diameter, enough to level most of a continent. the tsunamis created would cause massive destruction, and nuclear fallout would be planet-wide.

that said, yes humanity could probably survive it, just the world would be a sucky place to live in the meantime.

meanwhile the "planetary evacuation insufficient" was saying if the two completely failed to annihilate each other, thus referring to the question of what DOES happen when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object. what if both truly have an infinite amount of energy between them and are totally indestructible? then where does the energy go? what happens? this could potentially cause a release of energy powerful enough to wipe out the universe, or create a black hole, or cause reality to cease, or any number of POSSIBLE scenarios. but of course that part is redacted because your imagination for that will be better than my own.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Megatons is fine. A megaton of TNT is a recognised unit of energy, equal to about 4.2MJ. No need to say "nuclear" though, just "explosion".

I'm guessing the Foundation's reasoning is that the worst case scenario would be the total conversion of the mass of both objects to energy, although according to the calculation I just did, assuming the balls are made of solid iron or something of equal density, that would actually yield about 100 gigatons.

That sounds like a heck of a lot, but it's unlikely that this would result in anything even approaching an end-of-world scenario. According to Wikipedia, the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake released about 9000 gigatons, and the earth is still in one piece.

To do some serious damage, you would need a lot more than that. The asteroid impact that killed the dinosaurs is estimated at about 96 teratons (96,000 gigatons). And that mostly just messed up the biosphere; the only damage to the earth itself was a 180km diameter crater.

To do something that would make "planetary evacuation insufficient" would require thinking much bigger.
